prompt: The second `GOCACHE=/tmp/cold go run -x . top -n 1 access.log` printed a single command, the path of an executable inside `/tmp/cold`. Why was there no compile and no link?
hint: Look at where that path points.

choices.text: The first `go run` stored its executable in the cache; this one ran it
choices.why: Right. The first run linked into `$WORK`, copied the result into the cache, and every later run with the same inputs starts the cached file.

choices.text: `go run` interprets the source when nothing has changed
choices.why: There is no interpreter in the go command. Even the first run compiled and linked; the path shows a real executable.

choices.text: It reused `./hits`, the binary that `go build -o hits` had written just before it
choices.why: The path it ran is inside `/tmp/cold`, not `./hits`. `go run` builds without debugger information, so the two executables are different files.

choices.text: `-x` only prints commands the first time
choices.why: `-x` prints every command that runs. The second run printed one line because one command ran.

prompt: A CI step runs `go run . count "$f"` and treats exit status 2 as "the job was misconfigured". The branch never fires, even when the command line is wrong. Why?
hint: `hits` itself does return 2 for a usage error.

choices.text: `go run` reports the child's status as a message and exits 1
choices.why: Right. `go run .` printed `exit status 2` and returned 1. Build the binary and run it when the exit code matters.

choices.text: A CI shell turns every non-zero exit status into 1 before the step sees it
choices.why: The shell passes statuses through unchanged; lesson 1's `./hits; echo $?` printed 2.

choices.text: `hits` returns 2 only when it is started from a terminal
choices.why: `run` returns 2 for a usage error whoever calls it; the table test in lesson 1 checked it with no terminal at all.

choices.text: The build failed first, so the program never ran
choices.why: The usage text was printed, so the program ran; it is the status on the way out that changed.

prompt: After `touch main.go internal/tally/tally.go`, how many package names did `GOCACHE=/tmp/cold go build -v -o hits .` print?
hint: `touch` changes the modification time and nothing else.

prompt: Starting in `~/daily` with no executable in it, which of these commands leave an executable file somewhere under `~/daily`? Choose every one that does.
hint: An executable is written only for exactly one `main` package, unless `-o` names a directory.

choices.text: `go build`
choices.why: Yes. One `main` package, in the current directory, so it writes `hits`, named after `example.com/hits`.

choices.text: `go build -o bin/ ./...`
choices.why: Yes. `-o` with a directory writes every `main` package of the list there: `bin/hits` and `bin/genlog`.

choices.text: `go build ./...`
choices.why: Three packages, so nothing is written: the command only checks that they build.

choices.text: `go build ./internal/tally`
choices.why: `tally` is not a `main` package. It is compiled into the cache and the result is discarded.

choices.text: `go run .`
choices.why: `go run` links into a temporary directory and keeps the executable in the build cache, which is under `~/.cache`, not `~/daily`.

prompt: Inside `~/daily`, `go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer` fails with `no required module provides package`. What does the message mean?
hint: Without a version, `go install` works in the context of the current module.

choices.text: The proxy has no module called `golang.org/x/tools`
choices.why: The same path with `@v0.52.0` downloaded at once. The module exists; `go.mod` just does not require it.

choices.text: `go.mod` requires nothing that contains this package
choices.why: Right. With no version the build uses this module's requirements, and `hits` has none. `@version` builds outside them.

choices.text: `stringer` is not a `main` package and cannot be installed
choices.why: It is a command; installed at a version it landed in `~/go/bin` and `go version -m` read it.

choices.text: `GOBIN` is unset, so there is nowhere to install to
choices.why: Unset `GOBIN` falls back to `~/go/bin`, where `hits` was installed a moment before.

prompt: After `go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer@v0.52.0` succeeded inside `~/daily`, what did `go.mod` contain?
hint: `cat go.mod` was run right after.

choices.text: A `require golang.org/x/tools v0.52.0` line
choices.why: That is what `go get` would add. An install with `@version` ignores the current module's `go.mod`.

choices.text: The same two lines as before
choices.why: Right. `module example.com/hits` and `go 1.27.1`, untouched: the tool is not a dependency of the code.

choices.text: A `tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer` line
choices.why: A `tool` line is what `go get -tool` writes, a different command chosen on purpose.

choices.text: Three `require` lines: x/tools, x/mod and x/sync
choices.why: Those three are inside the binary, as `go version -m` shows, and none of them reached `go.mod`.

prompt: For the `hits` installed from `~/daily`, `go version -m` printed `mod example.com/hits ___`: the version a module gets when it is built from a directory rather than fetched at a version.
hint: A word in parentheses.

prompt: A `Makefile` target runs `go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer@latest`. Two developers who ran it a month apart get different generated files from the same source. What is the fix?
hint: Which part of that command means something different next month?

choices.text: Run `go clean -i` before every install
choices.why: That removes the old executable and then installs whatever `@latest` means today; the drift stays.

choices.text: Drop the suffix and run it as plain `go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer`
choices.why: Without a version the build uses the project's `go.mod`, which does not require x/tools, and the command fails.

choices.text: Write the version out, `@v0.52.0`
choices.why: Right. A written version builds the same program on every machine; `@latest` is resolved again on each run.

choices.text: Set `GOBIN` to a directory inside the project
choices.why: That decides where the executable lands, not which version of it is built.

prompt: `go test ./...` printed `ok example.com/hits/internal/tally (cached)`. What happened to `tally`'s tests in that run?
hint: Compare the time column with the run before.

choices.text: They ran in less time than the clock could measure
choices.why: A run would print a time, as the first run did with 0.483 seconds. `(cached)` replaces the time because nothing ran.

choices.text: Only the tests whose code changed since the previous run were run again
choices.why: The cache works per package and test binary: either the whole result is reused or the binary runs.

choices.text: Nothing ran; the go command printed the result it had stored
choices.why: Right. Same test binary, cacheable flags: the stored output was printed again. `-count=1` forces a run.

choices.text: The tests were skipped, because `-short` is switched on by default in package list mode
choices.why: `-short` is off unless given; the skip message appears only with it.

prompt: `go test -run Top -v ./internal/tally` ran `TestTop` and also `ExampleTop`. Which pattern runs `TestTop` alone?
hint: The expression is a regular expression, and it is not anchored.

choices.text: `-run Top$`
choices.why: Anchoring the end is half of it: `ExampleTop` also ends in `Top`, so both still run.

choices.text: `-run '^TestTop$'`
choices.why: Right. The anchors say the whole name, so `ExampleTop` no longer matches.

choices.text: `-run Top -list .`
choices.why: `-list` prints names and runs nothing at all.

choices.text: `-run Top -failfast`
choices.why: `-failfast` changes what happens after a failure, not which tests match.

prompt: A row named `short line` in `TestParse`'s table runs as the subtest `TestParse/___` in the `-v` output.
hint: Spaces in a subtest name are replaced.

prompt: A test in `tally` reads `testdata/sample.log`, a file inside the module. You edit that file and run `go test ./...` again, with no other change. What does the `tally` line show?
hint: `go help test` names what else a cached result depends on.

choices.text: A time: the content of a file the test reads is part of the cache key
choices.why: Right. For files opened within the module, the cache key includes their content, so an edit makes the old result miss.

choices.text: `(cached)`, because the Go source did not change
choices.why: That is the belief the cache rule was written to avoid: files inside the module and environment variables the test reads are part of the key.

choices.text: `(cached)` until somebody runs `go clean -testcache` to throw the old result away
choices.why: Clearing works, but it is not needed here: the edited file already invalidates the result.

choices.text: `[no test files]`, because the go command ignores everything under a `testdata` directory
choices.why: `testdata` is ignored as a package directory, which is why it holds fixtures; the test files of `tally` are still there.

prompt: Match each `go test` flag with what it did to `tally`'s tests.
hint: One description belongs to no flag here.

pairs.right: no new test started after `TestParse/good` failed
the package ran although a cached result existed
four names printed and nothing run

right_distractors: the tests ran in a random order

prompt: Why did `go doc tally.summary`, all in lowercase, print the type `Summary`?
hint: `go help doc` has a rule about case.

choices.text: Lowercase letters in the argument match either case
choices.why: Right. Uppercase letters match exactly and lowercase ones match both, so `summary` finds `Summary`.

choices.text: `go doc` lowercases every name before it searches
choices.why: Then `go doc Foo` could not be told from a package path, and the help says an uppercase start means a symbol in the current directory.

choices.text: Go identifiers are case-insensitive
choices.why: They are case-sensitive: the case of the first letter decides whether a name is exported.

choices.text: There is an unexported `summary` that documents the type
choices.why: `tally` declares no such name; `go doc` matched the exported type.

prompt: Put these four packages in the order `go list -deps .` prints them for `hits`.
hint: A package is printed after everything it imports.

prompt: `go list` put `main_test.go` in `TestGoFiles` and `tally_test.go` in `XTestGoFiles`. What decides which list a test file goes in?
hint: Read the first line of each file.

choices.text: Whether the file sits at the module root or in a subdirectory
choices.why: The directory decides which package's lists it appears in, not which of the two lists.

choices.text: Its package clause: the package itself, or the package name with `_test` added
choices.why: Right. `package main` is an in-package test; `package tally_test` is compiled as a separate package that imports `tally`.

choices.text: Whether it contains examples as well as tests
choices.why: Examples can live in either kind of test file; `ExampleTop` is in `tally_test.go` by choice.

choices.text: Whether the file tests a `main` package
choices.why: A library can have both kinds; it is the package clause, not what is under test.

prompt: A log arrives with one request whose URL is 100,000 characters long, on line 7 of 20,000. What does `hits count` do with that file?
hint: `go doc bufio.MaxScanTokenSize` printed the limit, and `Count` never calls `Buffer`.

choices.text: Counts the other 19,999 lines and skips the long one
choices.why: `Count` stops at the first error and returns it; nothing in `hits` skips a line.

choices.text: Reports `bufio.Scanner: token too long` and exits 1, with no table
choices.why: Right. A line over 64 KiB stops the `Scanner`, and `summarise` prints the error and returns 1, as the 70,000-byte line did.

choices.text: Reads the line in pieces and reports it as 5 malformed lines
choices.why: The `Scanner` does not split an over-long line; it gives up with an error.

choices.text: Panics, because `Buffer` was never called
choices.why: `Buffer` panics only when called after scanning started. Not calling it leaves the default limit.

prompt: `go list -deps . | wc -l` printed 80 for `hits`, and the template that hides the standard library printed two lines. How many standard library packages go into `hits`?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: A CI job runs `go build ./...` and then a step that runs `./hits count sample.log`. The second step fails with `No such file or directory`. What is wrong?
hint: Count the packages that `./...` names in this module.

choices.text: The build cache was empty on the CI machine
choices.why: An empty cache makes the build slower, not absent; the result would still be written.

choices.text: `./...` excludes the root package
choices.why: It includes the root: `go list ./...` printed `example.com/hits` first.

choices.text: With several packages `go build` writes nothing; `go build -o bin/ ./...` or `go build -o hits .` writes the file
choices.why: Right. Three packages make it a check only. Name one `main` package, or give `-o` a directory.

choices.text: The executable went to `~/go/bin`
choices.why: That is `go install`. `go build` never writes to `GOBIN`.

prompt: A teammate asks which directory the compiler reads `internal/tally` from, because they suspect a stale copy. Which command answers exactly that?
hint: One of these prints a field of the package structure.

choices.text: `go doc -src tally.Top`
choices.why: It prints the source of one declaration, not where the package's files live.

choices.text: `go env GOCACHE`
choices.why: That names where compiled results are kept, not the source the compiler reads.

choices.text: `go list -f '{{.Dir}}' ./internal/tally`
choices.why: Right. `.Dir` is the directory containing the package sources the build uses: `/home/ana/daily/internal/tally` here.

choices.text: `go version -m ./bin/hits`
choices.why: It names modules and versions inside a binary, not directories.
